strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: MLIPs trained only on E/F/stress constrain PES curvature only indirectly, and the paper first establishes (Fig. 2) that Hessian error correlates with errors in phonon-derived thermodynamic properties, providing empirical grounding for the method.

The scalable training strategy is technically sound: stochastic sampling of one Hessian column per structure combined with a single Hessian-vector product reduces per-step cost from O(N^2) to O(N), making direct curvature supervision feasible for the large supercells required by finite-displacement phonon calculations. The 'triple-backward' implementation details are explained.

The key ablation is convincing: directly fine-tuning on the underlying displacement E/F/S data (which nominally contains the Hessian information) actually worsens Hessian error, demonstrating that the second-derivative loss itself, not merely extra phonon data, drives the improvement.

Evaluation is broad and honest: held-out MDR Phonon test set (1,000 materials, with careful splitting so gains come from phonon information rather than novel chemistry), Matbench Discovery thermal conductivity (0.446 to 0.306 kSRME, showing transfer to third-order derivatives), Matbench stability (co-training preserves F1 within 1% vs. a 60% drop without), and elastic properties in the appendix.

The co-training recipe is simple, well-motivated (phonon data is equilibrium-biased), and ablated; the paper transparently reports that co-training costs some Hessian accuracy and that neither PFT variant improves Matbench Discovery over the base model.

Reproducibility support is good: hyperparameters, selection rationale, compute budgets (140 vs 60 A100-hours), and an analysis of the MDR Phonon vs. MPtrj energy discrepancy are provided; code, weights, and preprocessed data are stated to be released.
Honest discussion of limitations: reliance on AD-capable frameworks (JAX), equilibrium bias of phonon datasets, and the need for continued-learning strategies.
weaknesses: Only one architecture (Nequix MP) is fine-tuned, yet the method is claimed to be 'model agnostic'; demonstrating PFT on at least one other backbone (e.g., MACE or eSEN) would substantially strengthen the generality claim, especially since the authors note sampling/augmentation considerations may differ for non-equivariant models.

The headline correlation between Hessian error and phonon property error (Fig. 2) and thermal conductivity (Fig. 5) rests on only ~6 model points; this is suggestive rather than statistically robust, and correlation across a handful of models does not strictly establish that reducing Hessian loss causes property improvements (though the fine-tuning results do support this).

Novelty relative to closely related work is incremental: Amin et al. (2025) already sample random Hessian columns for Hessian-based training (via JVPs on direct-force models), and Fang et al. (2024) trained on Hessians via AD; the contribution here is adapting this to energy-conserving models with HVPs plus co-training, which is useful but not a fundamentally new technique.

Some training details appear ad hoc: the force-constant weight is 'not tuned, selected to be larger than other weights,' the phonon energy weight is set to 0 in the co-trained model, force/stress labels are assumed zero by construction, and energies are synthesized by multiplying unit-cell energies by supercell repetitions; sensitivity analyses for these choices are not provided, so the robustness of the recipe to other datasets/models is unclear.
The 'Code and Data' section contains no actual URL/link in the manuscript, weakening verifiable reproducibility at review time.

Small apparent inconsistencies: the claim of 55% average improvement is computed relative to Nequix MP only, while 'state-of-the-art' comparisons are against models that differ greatly in size and training data (e.g., eSEN-30M); also minor over-claiming in text (e.g., 'can could', elasticity text says 'performance on both modulus is improved' while bulk modulus K MAE worsened).
Fixed co-training ratio K=4 and 200 epochs are based on GPU budget rather than tuning; no sensitivity analysis of K is given, though the paper itself notes K can be tuned by monitoring validation.

strengths: The core technical idea is sound and well-executed: supervising PES curvature by matching MLIP Hessians to DFT-derived force constants, with stochastic Hessian column sampling reduced to a single Hessian-vector product (Eq. 10, Sec. 3.3), which reduces per-step cost from O(N^2) to O(N) and makes training on large phonon supercells feasible. This is a practical, useful contribution to the materials ML community.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough: Table 1 shows consistent improvements across four phonon thermodynamic metrics (e.g., ω_max MAE drops from 24 to 12 K), Fig. 3 includes a meaningful ablation showing that directly fine-tuning on phonon displacement EFS data actually worsens Hessian error (an interesting and non-obvious finding), and the extension to third-order derivatives via thermal conductivity (κ_SRME 0.446 → 0.306, Table 2) supports the claim of generalization beyond second-order properties.

The co-training scheme is validated: Table 3 shows catastrophic forgetting without it (F1 collapses from 0.751 to 0.301) versus <1% degradation with it, and the hyper-parameter appendix (A.2) documents selection rationale with commendable honesty (e.g., λ_Φ 'not tuned', epochs 'based on GPU budget').

The paper is clearly written, the methodology (Secs. 2-3) is accessible to non-experts in lattice dynamics, and code, weights, and preprocessed data are promised for release, supporting reproducibility. The MDR/MPtrj energy discrepancy analysis (A.1) is a useful diagnostic for the community.
The limitations discussion (Sec. 6) is honest: it acknowledges equilibrium bias of phonon datasets, the need for AD infrastructure, and that co-training is a continual-learning necessity.
weaknesses: Generality is claimed but demonstrated on only a single base model (Nequix MP, 707K params). The abstract and discussion present PFT as 'model agnostic', but no results show it transfers to other architectures (e.g., MACE, SevenNet) or stronger base models, and the paper itself notes sampling considerations differ for non-equivariant architectures (Sec. 3.2). The SOTA claim is carefully scoped to MPtrj-trained models, but this scoping is easy to miss.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work. The related work section concedes that Fang et al. (2024) trained on Hessians via AD and Amin et al. (2025) also randomly sample Hessian columns for training. The remaining novel elements — stochastic column sampling for periodic supercells via HVP and co-training — are useful engineering but not a fundamental advance. A more direct empirical comparison to at least Amin et al.'s approach would strengthen the contribution.

Some methodological assumptions are under-justified: force and stress labels for phonon displacement structures are assumed to be exactly zero (Sec. 4.1), and the energy label is reconstructed by scaling unitcell energies, despite the documented energy discrepancy between MDR Phonon and MPtrj (A.1, MAE 31.6 meV/atom with outliers up to 1.5 eV/atom). The impact of these choices on the fine-tuned model is not quantified.

No statistical uncertainty is reported for the headline results. Table 1 results on 1,000 test materials would support error bars or significance tests, and the differences between PFT with/without co-training (e.g., F: 5 vs 4 kJ/mol) may not be meaningful; the paper's phrasing ('slight improvement') acknowledges this but does not resolve it.

Some evaluation breadth is thin: thermal conductivity is evaluated on the Matbench Discovery set with a fixed 0.03 Å displacement, but only two qualitative examples (Fig. 6) of macroscopic κ are shown; the elastic property results in A.3 are mixed (bulk modulus worsens: 15.03 → 16.49 GPa MAE) and are relegated to the appendix without discussion in the main text.

Writing contains enough minor issues (e.g., broken reference '(Miranda)', typo in Eq. 9, 'which can could cause' in Sec. 3.4, an empty code URL placeholder in the Code and Data section) to slightly undercut polish, and the empty code link is a reproducibility concern if not fixed before camera-ready.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper connects the known PES-curvature softening of EFS-trained universal MLIPs (Deng et al., 2025) to degraded phonon predictions, and empirically demonstrates a strong correlation between Hessian error and phonon property error (Figs. 2 and 5).

The core technical recipe is sound and well-executed: stochastic Hessian column sampling with a single Hessian-vector product reduces per-step cost from O(N²) to O(N), enabling training on large phonon supercells; the batched-HVP implementation detail is genuinely useful for practitioners.

Strong empirical results: 55% average error reduction across phonon thermodynamic properties on the MDR Phonon benchmark, state-of-the-art thermal conductivity (κSRME 0.306 vs. 0.446 baseline) among MPtrj-trained models, and a useful demonstration that gains transfer to third-order derivatives.

Thoughtful ablations: comparison against naive fine-tuning on phonon displacement data (which performs worse), co-training vs. no co-training (Fig. 3, Table 3), and analytical vs. finite-displacement force-constant evaluation (Table 1) all support the design choices.

Good reproducibility: code, trained weights, and preprocessed data are released; hyperparameters, their selection rationale, and a candid analysis of the MPtrj/MDR energy discrepancy (Appendix A.1) are documented.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper openly reports that PFT does not improve Matbench Discovery stability, that phonon data is biased to equilibrium geometries, and that non-equivariant architectures may need different sampling strategies.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: Hessian-based training (Fang et al., 2024), stochastic Hessian column sampling (Amin et al., 2025), and catastrophic-forgetting mitigation via data interleaving are all established techniques. The contribution is largely an application/combination of these to materials foundation-model fine-tuning rather than a new methodological idea.

Evaluation on a single base model: all results fine-tune only Nequix MP (707K params, the smallest model considered). The claim that PFT is 'model agnostic' is untested; it is unclear whether the approach works for larger or architecturally different models (MACE, eSEN, GNoME-style), or whether the gains are specific to this small, possibly under-converged base model.

The headline 'state-of-the-art across all metrics' needs qualification: eSEN-MP matches or beats the co-trained PFT model on entropy and Helmholtz free energy (Table 1); only the non-co-trained variant is uniformly best, and it pays a 60% F1 degradation on stability classification.
The correlation evidence in Fig. 2 rests on only six models; this is suggestive but statistically thin support for the central claim that Hessian error drives property error.

Some methodological approximations are not fully validated: assuming zero forces and stresses on displacement structures, and the unmotivated choice λΦ=100 ('not tuned') and K=4 co-training ratio, leave sensitivity to key hyperparameters unexplored.

Training and evaluation are limited to PBE-level data, so conclusions about phonon accuracy inherit the accuracy ceiling of that functional level, and the test materials overlap heavily with the upstream pretraining distribution (by design), leaving generalization to novel chemistries unaddressed.

Presentation issues remain: several typos and incomplete sentences ('trained with standard a standard loss', 'can could cause forgetting', truncated sentence in Sec. 3.4), and the definition of L_Φ (Eq. 9) mixes sampled and summed indices in a way that requires careful reading.
